newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Russia may help Bulgaria complete new reactor.
newsitem.headline: Russia may help Bulgaria complete new reactor.

text.p: Russia is ready to participate in a consortium for the eventual completion of Bulgaria's second nuclear power station at Belene together with Germany's Siemens AG and France's Framatome, a senior Russian official said on Thursday.
Yurii Vishnevskii, president of Russia's atomic and radiation safety federal supervisory body signed a cooperation agreement on Thursday with his Bulgarian counterpart Lachezar Kostov.

"I hope that we can participate in a consortium for the completion of the Belene unit. This is profitable for Bulgaria and Russia," Vishnevskii said, adding that Russia could supply the reactor's equipment.
"Siemens and Framatome have shown a great interest (in participating in the Belene construction) and we have scientific and practical relations with them," he said.

Vishnevskii, who will visit Belene on Friday, said Siemens' electric equipment was better than Russia's. He also praised Framatome's projects for thermal-mechanical parts, as well as for turbine parts.
"That is why a consortium is profitable for all," he said.
Work on the construction of the Belene plant, 250 km (160 miles) north of Sofia, started in the 1980s but was stopped six years ago due to a shortage of money and protests of environmentalists.
The foundations of the plant have been built up and a 1,000-megawatt Soviet-designed reactor is on site. Some $1 billion has been invested there.
Under Bulgaria's long-term energy programme, the development of the energy sector will require the completion of the Belene plant if the government decides to go ahead with it.
Vishnevskii stressed that Russia could make some investment in the unit's construction. "But it will be difficult for us to invest 100 percent," he said.
Apart from Siemens and Framatome, U.S.-based Westinghouse Electric Corp has shown interest in providing advanced technology for the Belene plant.

Bulgaria, which is poor in energy resources, relies for almost half of its energy needs on its Soviet-designed Kozloduy nuclear power plant, which has four VVER 440-megawatt reactors and two 1,000-megawatt reactors.
But the projected life of its four reactors will expire within the next 10 years and the country is expected to need more than 1,500 megawatts by that time, officials said.

Sofia closed its oldest reactor, number one, on May 15 for checks on its vessel's metal following strong international pressure. It hopes to receive preliminary results on the metal's safety from Russia's Korchatov Institute in November.
Russia, Siemens, Framatome and Westinghouse have also said they are prepared to upgrade the Kozloduy plant.
